newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM says Europe will be goal after polls.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM says Europe will be goal after polls.

text.p: Slovenia's drive to play its part at the heart of Europe as a member of the European Union and NATO will remain a top government priority after next month's general election, Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said.

Speaking at a lakeside hotel in the Alpine resort of Bled, Drnovsek listed Slovenia's economic strength, political stability and its geostrategic position on the balance sheet for the country's swift integration into Europe.

"Full membership of the European Union will remain a priority...of the incoming government," the prime minister told Reuters in an interview late on Thursday. "Slovenia has also met all the criteria to become a NATO member."

His government had received signals from a majority of NATO's 16 member states that it was likely to be included in the first expansion of the military alliance next year. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the other frontrunners.

Polls show Drnovsek's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is expected to remain the biggest party in a general election on November 10 -- the second free poll since Slovenia declared independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.

Drnovsek, who was president of federal Yugoslavia between 1989 and 1990, said his Liberal Democrats had not excluded any party as a potential coalition partner. His fragile coalition with the Christian Democrats almost collapsed last May.
He said the rightist People's Party and right-wing Social Democrats must drop their opposition to constitutional change to adapt to EU membership if they wanted to enter government.
"In opposition it is easy to use populist language to say foreigners are going to buy up the whole of Slovenia."
The premier said he understood the concerns of international investors over the slow pace of legislation on foreign investment but vowed to speed up reform.
He acknowledged that Slovenia still suffered a pyschological barrier over accepting foreign firms on its soil.
"There is a belief in Slovenian public opinion and among certain parties that we should protect ourselves," he said. "But this will change."

He confidently predicted that Slovenia would meet the criteria laid down in the Maastricht treaty for European economic and monetary union by its planned entry date of 2001, but said this would mean further cuts in public spending.
"We will have to check our social welfare transfers to see if these are sustainable," he said.
The former communists, the United List of Social Democrats, could pick up support from Slovenians worried about their jobs and welfare benefits in the November elections.
Despite plaudits from abroad over Slovenia's democratic stability, human rights groups have criticised the government for its treatment of non-Slovene citizens.

The International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights said in its 1996 report that thousands of people born in other Yugoslav republics were being denied citizenship, even though they had lived in Slovenia for years.
Drnovsek said Slovenia had been generous in granting citizenship to 190,000 people since 1991 but agreed the processing of applications had been slow in some cases.
"If they meet the criteria, they will get citizenship," he said.
